result.summary: Alcinous calls an assembly, arranges a ship for Ulysses and holds a feast where the bard Demodocus sings and Ulysses weeps. At the games Euryalus insults Ulysses, who throws the disc far beyond the rest; Demodocus sings of Mars and Venus, and gifts are given. Ulysses weeps again at the song of Troy's fall, and Alcinous asks him to say who he is.

scenes.title: Assembly and preparations for escort
scenes.summary: Alcinous calls the Phaeacians together, with Minerva's help, and orders a ship readied and a feast prepared.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses needs the Phaeacians' escort to get home.

scenes.title: Feast and Demodocus's first song
scenes.summary: The ship is readied and the feast held. Demodocus sings of the quarrel of Ulysses and Achilles, and Ulysses weeps; Alcinous notices and proposes games.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks revealing his identity through his tears.

scenes.title: The games and Ulysses' challenge
scenes.summary: The Phaeacians compete. Euryalus taunts Ulysses, who hurls a huge disc past every mark and boasts of his skills.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses' honour as a guest and his pride are at stake.

scenes.title: Alcinous calls for dancing
scenes.summary: Alcinous soothes Ulysses and boasts of Phaeacian dancing and music. Dancers take the ground and Demodocus returns.

scenes.title: Song of Mars and Venus
scenes.summary: Demodocus sings how Vulcan trapped Mars and Venus in chains. The gods laughed, Neptune pledged payment, and the lovers were freed.
scenes.stakes: Vulcan's honour as a betrayed husband; Mars and Venus face public shame.

scenes.title: Dancing and gifts
scenes.summary: Laodamas and Halius dance with a ball. Alcinous orders gifts for Ulysses and Euryalus apologises with a sword.

scenes.title: Bath, chest and Nausicaa
scenes.summary: Arete packs the gifts, Ulysses bathes, and Nausicaa bids him remember her. He sends meat to Demodocus.

scenes.title: Song of the wooden horse
scenes.summary: Ulysses asks for the tale of the wooden horse. Demodocus sings the sack of Troy and Ulysses weeps like a captured widow.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses' grief threatens to expose him.

scenes.title: Alcinous asks his name
scenes.summary: Alcinous stops the song and asks Ulysses his name, country and travels, mentioning the ships that steer themselves and Neptune's threat.
scenes.stakes: Phaeacia risks Neptune's wrath for escorting strangers.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses rebukes Euryalus, noting that the gods do not grace all men alike.
Alcinous says the gods send misfortunes so future generations have something to sing about.

analysis.text: Ulysses' tears at songs of his own past show the gap between his hidden identity and his fame, leading to his self-revelation.
The games and the bard reflect the Homeric ideals of hospitality, athletic prowess and oral song in a feasting hall.

legacy.text: The tale of Mars and Venus caught in Vulcan's net was retold by Ovid in the Metamorphoses and often painted in the Renaissance.

fun_facts.text: Many readers have taken the blind bard Demodocus as a self-portrait of Homer, a long-standing tradition.

language_notes.text: "Child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn" is a Homeric formula for daybreak, repeated throughout the poem.
"Aldermen and town councillors" is the translator's Victorian rendering for the Phaeacian leaders and nobles; the original has no such offices.
"Either East or West" means from anywhere at all; Alcinous does not know where the stranger comes from.
"Escort" means conveyance home, here by ship, which the Phaeacians were famous for providing.
"I will find you in everything" means Alcinous will provide all supplies for the feast. The "65" is a stray footnote number.
"Cloisters" here means the covered colonnades or halls of the palace.
Thole-pins are upright pegs set in a boat's side that act as pivots for the oars; the thongs tie the oars to them.
"66" is a stray footnote marker from the edition, not part of the story. "Out houses" means outbuildings around the main house.
"To wit" is an archaic phrase meaning "that is to say"; "in the mouths of all men" means widely talked about.
Pytho is Delphi, site of Apollo's oracle. Agamemnon was told the Trojan war would begin when the best Greeks quarrelled.
A drink-offering (libation) is wine poured out to the gods; "lays" are songs or poems.
"Aldermen and town councillors" is the translator's modern rendering of the Phaeacian chiefs and counsellors.
Cloister here means the covered colonnade or hall of the palace, not a monastery.
The footnote marker 67 points to a translator's note; the distance is measured by a plough-furrow, a common ancient unit of length.
Euryalus insults Ulysses by comparing him to a merchant; Phaeacians prized athletics and saw trading for profit as lowly.
"Conversation" here means manner and speech in general; "honeyed moderation" means sweet, measured eloquence.
"Stung me to the quick" means wounded deeply, to the most sensitive part.
"Have a bout with me" means have a contest or fight.
"Cut the ground from under his own feet" means ruin his own position, here by offending his host.
Philoctetes was a famed Greek archer at Troy, who held the bow of Hercules.
Eurytus of Oechalia was a legendary archer; Hercules is Greek heroes' greatest strongman and also a bowman.
Eurytus challenged Apollo, god of archery, to a contest and was killed for his presumption.
"Apprehend my meaning" means understand what I intend; Alcinous is tactfully telling Ulysses to report the Phaeacians' good qualities, not the insult.
"Linen" here means clothing; frequent changes of clothes signal luxury.
"Foot and trip it" is an old idiom for dancing lightly and quickly.
"Smithy" is a blacksmith's forge; "toils" and "snare" elsewhere mean net or trap.
The Sintians were a people of Lemnos; "barbarous" here means they spoke a foreign tongue, not that they were savage.
Vulcan refers to the bride-price he paid Jove for Venus, which he now demands back as damages.
"Cast in heavy damages" means Mars will be legally fined for adultery, a compensation due to the wronged husband.
"A bad man's bond is bad security" is a proverb: a pledge made for a worthless person is a poor guarantee.
Thrace was associated with Mars, and Paphos in Cyprus was a principal cult site of Venus.
"Aldermen and town councillors" is the translator's Victorian rendering of the Phaeacian chiefs; the Greek has a more general term for leaders and counsellors.
A talent of gold was a measure of weight; in Homer it is a modest unit of gold, not a fixed coin.
"May the winds blow it away" is a wish that any offensive words be carried off and forgotten, a ritual way of cancelling an insult.
"Father stranger" is a respectful address to an older guest.
"Girded" means fastened on with a belt or strap; the sword hung from a baldric over the shoulder.
A "copper" here means a copper cauldron or large vessel for heating water, not the metal alone.
A tripod is a three-legged cauldron or stand placed over the fire to heat water.
Circe was the enchantress who hosted Ulysses for a year and taught him a knot; it is mentioned earlier in the epic.
Calypso was the nymph who kept Ulysses on her island for years before the gods ordered his release.
"Bearing-posts" are pillars holding up the roof of the cloister, the covered colonnade.
"Ransom" here means a repayment or thank-offering owed for saving his life.
"Lays" are songs or poems; Demodocus's song of Troy has made Ulysses weep.
Achaeans is one of Homer's names for the Greeks as a whole; Argives, used in sentence 157, is another.
Stratagem means a clever trick or scheme; here it is the deception of hiding warriors inside the horse.
The Greeks had burned their camp and sailed off, pretending to retreat, so the Trojans would take the horse as an offering.
Propitiation means an offering meant to win the gods' favour and avert their anger.
Ambuscade is an ambush, a hidden position from which an attack is sprung.
"Aldermen and town councillors" is the translator's Victorian-style rendering of the Phaeacian chiefs and counsellors; no such civic offices are meant literally.
"Affect no more concealment" means stop pretending or putting on reserve; Alcinous asks Ulysses to stop hiding his identity.
"Shape their purpose accordingly" means the ships will set their course to suit the destination named.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) resents the Phaeacians' escorts because they help travellers he may be punishing, such as Ulysses.
Argive Danaans are the Greeks who fought at Troy; both names are common Homeric terms for the Greek army.
The idea that gods send suffering so that poets will have songs to sing is a recurring Homeric view of epic poetry.

context_notes.text: Minerva (the Greek Athena) protects Ulysses and often acts by disguising herself as a mortal.
Demodocus is the blind bard of the Phaeacians; his songs will soon move Ulysses to tears.
Demodocus is a blind court singer. Bards in Homeric society were honoured, and they were thought to be inspired by the Muses.
Ulysses has not yet revealed his identity to the Phaeacians, so he hides his tears at hearing his own story sung.
Mars is the god of war; comparing a man to him praises his strength and bearing.
A suppliant was a person seeking protection and help, which hospitality customs obliged hosts to give.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) is Ulysses' divine protector and often appears disguised as a mortal.
Mars is the god of war and Venus the goddess of love; Vulcan, the lame smith god, is her husband.
The sun sees everything as he travels across the sky, so he is the natural informer.
Neptune is god of the sea; Mercury is the divine messenger; Apollo is god of music, prophecy and archery.
The Graces were minor goddesses of beauty and charm who attended Venus.
Ball-playing combined with dance was a favoured Phaeacian pastime, showing their leisure and skill. Polybus is named as the craftsman.
Euryalus had earlier insulted Ulysses by calling him a trader rather than an athlete, so the king demands amends.
Gifts were a central part of guest-friendship (xenia); the queen Arete keeps them safe in the palace.
Drink offerings (libations) were wine poured out to the gods before or during meals, so the goblet will keep Alcinous in Ulysses' mind.
Guests carried treasure home by ship, so theft while the traveller slept was a real concern.
Juno (the Greek Hera) is Jove's wife and queen of the gods.
Epeus was the Greek craftsman who built the wooden horse, helped by Minerva (the Greek Athene), goddess of craft and strategy.
Deiphobus was a Trojan prince who married Helen after Paris died. Menelaus, Helen's first husband, joined Ulysses in attacking his house.
Ulysses is still unrecognized at the Phaeacian court, so his weeping at a story about himself puzzles no one but Alcinous.
Guests and suppliants were under the protection of Jove, so hospitality was a sacred duty in the Greek world.
The Phaeacians were legendary sailors whose magical ships needed no pilots, which marks their land as semi-divine.

literary_notes.text: The fixed description of Dawn is a Homeric epithet, marking time's passage in a familiar, ritual way.
Mention of the coming trials of skill anticipates the athletic games that give the book its title.
Alcinous presents himself as a generous, proud host, reflecting Phaeacian hospitality.
The muse's gifts of song and blindness are set against each other, presenting the bard's talent and loss as a paired fate.
The audience knows the weeping guest is Ulysses, the song's hero, while the Phaeacians do not.
Alcinous alone notices the stranger's grief, showing him as perceptive and considerate as a host.
Ulysses turns Euryalus's insult back on him, calling the handsome man a fool, showing looks do not guarantee wisdom.
Throwing without even removing his cloak shows Ulysses' confidence and power despite claimed weariness.
The Phaeacians "quailed" beneath the flight itself, as if the disc's rushing were a force to be feared.
Minerva exaggerates that even a blind man could find the mark, stressing how far beyond the others it lies.
The story of Eurytus warns against challenging gods, anticipating the limits of boasting among powerful hosts.
The Phaeacians boast of luxury and dancing right after an athlete's insult, subtly answering the charge of softness.
Chains compared to cobwebs convey how fine and invisible the trap is.
"Givers of all good things" is a stock title for the gods, ironic beside their mocking laughter at the scene.
The gods' maxim turns the cuckolded cripple's victory into a moral lesson about cunning beating strength.
Mercury's bawdy boast lightens the mood and shows the gods' frivolous, all-too-human attitude to adultery.
Vivid physical detail of the red ball, the backward bend and the leap makes the game visible and graceful.
Ulysses' polite wish that Euryalus not miss the sword is gently ironic, a courteous way of accepting the apology while recalling the earlier insult.
Calypso's care is compared to the way a god would be tended, showing how thoroughly she looked after him.
Nausicaa's brief, bold farewell shows her as gracious and quietly hopeful, claiming her due as his rescuer.
Ulysses honours the bard whose song made him weep, showing his courtesy and his respect for poetry's divine source.
The remark that the city was doomed when it took in the horse points to Troy's coming destruction.
Comparing Ulysses to Mars, god of war, conveys his fury and violence in the sack of Troy.
Ulysses' grief is compared at length to a widow's, an unexpected image that casts the conquering warrior as a victim of war.
Ulysses, a conqueror of Troy, weeps as the conquered do, reversing his role and showing the suffering war brings to victors too.
Alcinous' gentle, reasoned appeal about names shows him as courteous and tactful, pressing his guest without offending him.
The self-steering ships that read their crews' thoughts and cannot be wrecked are marvellous exaggeration, showing the Phaeacians' wondrous, almost godlike seafaring.
The father's prophecy that Neptune will wreck a ship and bury the city under a mountain anticipates the later fate of the Phaeacians.
